issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette: Julian was twenty-one when he returned from three months as a relief worker in a fractured Middle Eastern province. He had traveled with a humanitarian coalition, carrying medical supplies and water purification tablets to displaced families. On his final week, the convoy route shifted without warning, and the compound where his team distributed aid came under sudden fire. In the chaos, voices rose in rapid, sharp Arabic from nearby rooftops and alleys. Men in uniforms and civilians alike sprinted past his position, their movements jerking and unpredictable. When a stranger's hand brushed Julian's shoulder while directing him toward cover, Julian froze, certain he was being singled out. The explosion that followed left a ringing silence and a scene so violent, so absolute, that it felt impossible. He had come to believe, in the weeks that followed, that the story of what happened that day could not possibly be true. Yet there he was, standing in the dust, the terror exactly as it had been, refusing to fade into memory. Back in his hometown, Julian took a position at a local Social Ministry, helping newly resettled families navigate housing applications and legal paperwork. The work demanded patience, but his nervous system no longer recognized ordinary surroundings as safe. Conversations at the center's break room about the war quickly became unbearable; the moment a colleague mentioned military strategy or equipment, Julian's pulse spiked and he would step out into the hallway until his breathing steadied. Even hearing Arabic shouted on a television screen or in the street beside him sent him into immediate guard. He could not separate the past from the present when recalling the incident. Sitting alone in his apartment, trying to tell his wife what had happened was as impossible as walking back into the compound. The words felt like opening a valve, flooding his body with the same panic he had experienced in the moment. Strangers in the grocery store or approaching him on the sidewalk were no longer just people; they were potential threats. He found himself tensing the instant a hand gestured toward him or someone stepped forward to ask for directions. Over months, his routines shifted in parallel, each habit carving deeper into his days. He delayed sleep, staying up until 3 a.m. to read or pace. Nights were broken by sudden awakenings; he would stand in the hallway, checking every lock, every window, until his fingers were numb and his breathing slowed. He ruminated relentlessly on how the incident could have been prevented. If only he had suggested a different supply route, if only he had spoken louder to his team leader, if only he had positioned himself differently, the outcome would not have been so irreversible. The guilt of those counterfactuals settled over him as a constant companion. Joyful moments grew difficult to inhabit. When the ministry team planned a weekend retreat, Julian declined, telling himself that letting himself feel hope would be disrespectful to what he had witnessed. He stopped looking at photographs of his deployment, avoiding any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, as though positivity required a betrayal of the event. At his office visit, Julian sat across from a clinician, his hands folded tightly in his lap. The ministry had noticed his absences, his distracted posture during client sessions, the way he flinched when a coworker reached for a file folder too quickly. He had come to this room because his wife gently but firmly told him he could no longer carry the isolation alone, and because he could no longer explain why he checked the doorframe three times before leaving for work. He was afraid that seeking help meant opening the same floodgates, that speaking aloud would make the terror permanent. Yet, beneath the fear, he hoped that someone might help him understand why his body still answered the world like a battlefield, and perhaps, just perhaps, allow him to live in the present again without feeling like an imposter in his own life.
